title: Lab 10 — Quiz 1
subtitle: Unknown ID Part 1 — specimens, MacConkey and citrate

questions.prompt: Which of these specimens comes from a 'typically sterile' body site?
questions.explanation: Typically sterile: blood, CSF, pleural, synovial and peritoneal fluid, urine before voiding, internal organ tissue. Growth from these is medically significant.

why.C: Stool contains large numbers of resident microbiota.
why.D: Voided urine picks up low numbers of urethral microbiota.

questions.prompt: Microbial growth from a blood culture should be considered:
questions.explanation: When samples from typically sterile sites are cultured from healthy people, nothing grows — so any growth is medically significant.

why.B: Growth from a sterile site is significant.
why.C: Any growth from a sterile site is significant.

questions.prompt: Patient A has fever, headache, sore throat, white patches in the throat and difficulty swallowing. Which specimen should be collected?
questions.explanation: Throat swabs are typically used for suspected Strep throat — aim for the inflamed tonsils and back of the throat.

why.A: Sputum is for suspected pneumonia or TB.

questions.prompt: Patient B has fever with chills, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain. Which specimen should be collected?
questions.explanation: Sputum is used for suspected pneumonia or TB: collect thick mucus from deep in the airway.

why.B: Throat swabs are for suspected Strep throat.
why.C: Saliva is thin and watery — avoid collecting it.

questions.prompt: Which sample is the CORRECT one to send for a suspected pneumonia culture?

options.text: Either sample — both work equally well
Neither — pneumonia is only diagnosed by blood

questions.explanation: Sputum: thick and sticky. Saliva: thin and watery. Avoid saliva to minimize resident microbiota.

why.A: Saliva is full of resident microbiota that outgrow pneumonia pathogens.
why.D: Sputum is the specimen for pneumonia or TB.

questions.prompt: Why are deep wound needle aspirates preferred over surface swabs, and how must they be handled?

options.text: Surface swabs pick up skin microbiota; aspirates must not be exposed to air
Surface swabs kill anaerobes; aspirates must be refrigerated
Aspirates are sterile; they can be held at room temperature for days
Swabs are too small; aspirates must be frozen right away

questions.explanation: Deep wound organisms can be anaerobic — specimens must not be exposed to air and are often cultured on reducing or other special media.

why.B: Deep wound organisms may be anaerobic, so they must not be exposed to air.
why.C: Specimens are protected from air and processed properly.
why.D: The issue is skin microbiota and anaerobes.

questions.prompt: Why can clean-catch urine specimens be refrigerated if they can't be processed right away?

options.text: Cold limits overgrowth of microbiota and doesn't harm UTI pathogens
Refrigeration kills all resident microbiota in urine
Cold temperatures make UTI pathogens grow faster
Urine from a clean catch is always sterile

questions.explanation: Process clean-catch urine ASAP or refrigerate it; UTI-causing pathogens aren't harmed by cold temperatures.

why.B: It slows overgrowth; it doesn't kill them.
why.C: Cold slows overgrowth; UTI pathogens simply survive it.
why.D: Clean-catch urine has low numbers of urethral microbiota.

questions.prompt: Which specimen must NEVER be refrigerated before culture?

options.text: A throat swab for Strep throat

questions.explanation: N. gonorrhoeae grows in culture but is easily killed by cold — never refrigerate a gonococcal specimen before culture.

why.B: This isn't the one singled out as never refrigerated.
why.D: Stool must be processed quickly, but gonococcal specimens are the 'never refrigerate' example.

questions.prompt: Read this MacConkey plate: pink colonies and pink medium. What does it tell you about this organism (E. coli)?
questions.explanation: MacConkey: growth = Gram-negative; pink = lactose fermenter (acid turns neutral red pink).

why.B: Gram-positives are inhibited and don't grow on MacConkey.
why.C: There is growth on this plate.

questions.prompt: Read this MacConkey plate: growth with yellow-orange colonies/medium. What does it tell you?
questions.explanation: This is Proteus mirabilis: it grows (Gram-negative) but doesn't ferment lactose (yellow-orange).

why.D: Citrate is read on citrate agar (blue).

questions.prompt: This MacConkey plate shows no growth (S. epidermidis). What can you conclude?

options.text: The plate was not incubated long enough

questions.explanation: Crystal violet and bile salts inhibit Gram-positives, so no growth = not Gram-negative.

why.B: A Gram-negative non-fermenter would still grow (yellow-orange).
why.C: No growth on MacConkey means not Gram-negative.

questions.prompt: Which components make MacConkey agar SELECTIVE?
questions.explanation: Selective: crystal violet + bile salts inhibit Gram-positives. Differential: lactose + neutral red.

why.C: Those are in mannitol salt agar.

questions.prompt: Read this citrate plate: growth, and the medium turned blue (S. marcescens). What is the result?
questions.explanation: Citrate agar: citrate is the sole carbon source; citrase producers grow and make basic byproducts that turn bromothymol blue BLUE.

why.B: Citrate negatives don't grow, so the medium stays green/teal.

questions.prompt: This citrate plate stayed green with no growth (Proteus mirabilis). What is the result?
questions.explanation: Citrase-negative organisms can't use citrate as their sole carbon source, so they don't grow and the medium stays green/teal.

why.A: Citrase positives grow and turn the medium blue.
why.C: Citrate agar tests citrase, not Gram reaction.

questions.prompt: In citrate agar, what is the pH indicator, and what color shows a positive result?
questions.explanation: Bromothymol blue turns blue when citrase breaks down citrate into alkaline (basic) byproducts.

why.A: Neutral red is the MacConkey indicator.
why.C: Phenol red is in MSA, TSI and fermentation broths.
